opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
“They feared the crowds, for they regarded him as a prophet.”
The religious leaders understood exactly what Jesus was saying. The Parable of the Tenants” was not obscure to them. The vineyard, the servants, the son—it was a mirror held up to their own history. They knew He was speaking about them.
And their first instinct was not reflection. It was removal. They wanted Him arrested. Silenced. Taken away.
But the Gospel says something revealing: they feared the crowds, because the people regarded Him as a prophet.
So the leaders hesitate—not because they question whether Jesus might be right, not because they reconsider their own hearts, but because they are calculating the reaction of the crowd.
It is a quiet but clear exposure of how power often works. Their concern is not truth, but consequence. Not whether Jesus is sent from God, but whether acting against Him would cost them influence.
They are trapped in a strange place: unwilling to follow Him, but also unwilling to oppose Him openly.
So nothing changes.
And in that moment, the Gospel reveals a tension that still exists in every age. A person can stand very close to truth—hear it clearly, recognize it even—and still remain unmoved if reputation, position, or control feels more important.
The crowds see a prophet.
The leaders see a threat.
And the tragedy is not that they failed to understand Jesus.
The tragedy is that they understood Him perfectly.
